case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Peel v. A.W.
text:
WARNING

The court hearing
this matter directs that the following notice should be attached to the file:

This is a case under Part V of the
Child, Youth and Family
Services Act, 2017
, (being Schedule 1 to the
Supporting Children, Youth
and Families Act, 2017
, S.O. 2017, c. 14), and is subject to subsections
87(7), 87(8) and 87(9) of the Act.
These subsections and subsection 142(3) of
the Act, which
deals with the consequences of
failure to comply, read as follows:

87.—
(7)
Order
excluding media representatives or prohibiting publication.
—   Where
the court is of the opinion that the presence of the media representative or
representatives or the publication of the report, as the case may be, would
cause emotional harm to a child who is a witness at or a participant in the
hearing or is the subject of the proceeding, the court may make an order,

.  .  .

(
c
)    prohibiting
the publication of a report of the hearing or a specified part of the hearing.

(8)
Prohibition re
identifying child.
—   No person shall publish or make public
information that has the effect of identifying a child who is a witness at or a
participant in a hearing or the subject of a proceeding, or the child’s parent
or foster parent or a member of the child’s family.

(9)
Prohibition re
identifying person charged
.—   The court may make an order
prohibiting the publication of information that has the effect of identifying a
person charged with an offence under this Part.

.   .   .

142.—
(3)
Offences
re publication.
—   A person who contravenes subsection 87(8)
or 134(11) (publication of identifying information) or an order prohibiting
publication made under clause 87(7)(
c
) or subsection 87(9), and a
director, officer or employee of a corporation who authorizes, permits or
concurs in such a contravention by the corporation, is guilty of an offence and
on conviction is liable to a fine of not more than $10,000 or to imprisonment
for a term of not more than three years, or to both.

ONTARIO COURT OF JUSTICE

CITATION:

Children’s Aid Society of Peel v. A.W.,
2025 ONCJ 130

DATE:
2025-03-07

20061/23
Brampton

BETWEEN:

THE CHILDREN’S AID
SOCIETY OF PEEL

Applicant

—
AND —

A.W.

—
AND —

S.W.

Respondents

Before
Justice Philip J. Clay

Heard
on November 25-December 2, 2024

Reasons
for Judgment released on March 7, 2025

Mr. K. Williams
.................................................................. counsel
for the applicant Society

Ms.  M. O’Connor
................................................ counsel
for the respondent Father, S.W.

Ms. M. Leonard
.......................................................................... counsel
for the child S.W.W.

The Respondent Mother
………………………………………….. A.W.,
on her own behalf

Ms. D. Stewart
…………………………...……………………………………

amicus
curiae

CLAY J
:

[
1
]

This child protection trial concerns the child S.W.W. born […], 2017.
A.W. is his mother and S.W. is his father.

[
2
]

The Applicant society sought an order for statutory and a child
protection finding and for a s. 102 order placing the child with his father.
The application before the court was an Amended Amended Protection Application
that was issued on September 17, 2024. The relief sought was supported by the
Respondent father S.W. (‘the father”) and by the Office of the Children’s
Lawyer (“OCL”). The Respondent mother A.W. (“the mother”) did not file an
Answer to any of the three protection Applications but her position was that
she sought an order returning the child to her care.

First trial motion

Relief
sought

[
3
]

At the outset of the hearing I was advised that the mother had served
and filed a Motion Form that sought to adjourn the trial and to lift the
requirement that leave be sought before further documents could be filed. The
Motion Form was served on November 14. No other party filed a responding
affidavit.

[
4
]

The mother said that she was self-represented and that she did not have
the time to properly prepare for trial. She said that the court’s leave
requirement prevented her from properly defending her case and she wanted it
removed.

[
5
]

The mother had not served and filed an Answer to the Amended or Amended
Amended Protection Applications and she had not filed briefs for any
conference. It appeared that the mother had attempted to file other documents
as “evidence” but her filings were rejected as not being authorized by the
Family
Law Rules
. She may well have been told that she required leave of the court
to file a document that was not permitted to be filed by the
Rules.

[
6
]

The mother’s Motion Form stated that the restrictions on filing limited
her defense and resulted in a lack of due process in that she was constrained
from filing documentation including witness statements and other relevant
evidence. She said that the constraints violated her right to a fair hearing
under the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. She referred to
numerous cases on the issue of due process, fair hearing and procedural
fairness. She said that the Supreme Court of Canada had emphasized the
importance of procedural fairness and the need for courts to accommodate the
unique challenges faced by self-represented persons. She said that the clerks
who did not permit her to file documents overstepped their role and
discriminated against her as a self-represented party.

[
7
]

The mother sought an adjournment and insisted on written reasons for the
decision on this motion prior to the trial proceeding.

Analysis

[
8
]

As the trial judge I had no prior involvement in this matter so I

reviewed
the issued orders and the endorsements in the Trial Record to see what
procedural steps had been taken prior to trial.

[
9
]

This child protection matter began with the return of a Protection
Application on December 13, 2023. The society sought a protection finding under
s. 74 (2) (h) of the
Child Youth and Family Services Act
based upon
evidence of emotional harm and the risk of emotional harm by the mother’s
parenting. The chronology of the proceeding was as follows:

December 13, 2023
–
Justice
M. Cheung without prejudice order placing child under supervision of the mother
with access to the father.

February 20, 2024  – Justice L. Rogers temporary order
after a temporary care and custody hearing placing child with the father with
supervised access to the mother initially twice a week for two hours.

April 17, 2024 – Justice Cheung – mother not present –
matter organized to be ready for trial sittings of September 9-20, 2024

June 17, 2024 – Justice Cheung- Settlement Conference
held – mother was present.

July 10, 2024 – Justice Cheung – scheduled Trial
Management Conference (“TMC”) could not proceed – mother had not filed any
documents and her behaviour resulted in her ultimately being removed from the
courtroom. Agreement by counsel for motion to appoint
amicus curiae
.

August 20, 2024 – Justice Cheung motion for
amicus

heard – all parties consented except mother who refused to make submissions but
repeatedly said “I am ready for September trial”. The matter was then targeted
for November 25-December 6, 2024 sittings with a preliminary TMC TBST on
September 18 and a final TMC on October 16, 2024 both in front of Justice
Cheung

August 29, 2024 – Justice Cheung released written
reasons on her decision to appoint
amicus curiae
. The case management
justice noted that the mother had not filed an Answer to the Protection Application,
the Amended Protection Application or the Amended Amended Protection
Application, had not been prepared for any conference and had disrupted
proceedings when present. She found that an
amicus
appointment was
necessary to give the mother someone to help her organize her case and to
ensure that all relevant evidence concerning the issues came before the court.

September 16, 2024 – Justice Cheung selected Ms.
Deborah Stewart from a list of experienced family law lawyers provided by LAO
to be
amicus curiae
in this case. Ms. Stewart reached out to the mother
to see if she could be of assistance but her emails were not returned.

September 18, 2024 – Justice Cheung – society advised
that it had served its Amended Amended Protection Application in which it
sought an order for a protection finding under s. 74 (2) (h) of the
CYFSA

-the risk of emotional harm by mother’s actions. If that order was made it
sought an order that the child be placed in the custody of the father subject
to s.102 of the
CYFSA
and that the mother should have access to the
child in the discretion of the father. The mother was very disruptive as she
insisted on reading aloud from a document and ignored the court’s direction.
Justice Cheung stepped off the bench and the mother left the court. Justice
Cheung said if that if the mother had not left she would have been removed. She
set out the ground rules for the mother’s continued participation in the case.

October 16, 2024 – Justice Cheung TMC issues defined,
witnesses identified, filing deadlines for society affidavits set. The mother
said that she would not participate in the time estimates for witnesses as she
would not be cross-examining.
Amicus
asked the court to set aside half a
day for the mother’s participation in the trial in the event it was requested
by her.

November 6, 2024 – Trial Audit before Justice Cheung
as LAJ – The mother said that she needed more time to get her witnesses
together and submit her documents. She said she might have upwards of twelve
witnesses. None had been disclosed. The mother was disruptive and talked over
other counsel. After receiving submissions Justice Cheung stated that the
mother could provide a list of not more than 5 witnesses by November 20 and she
must provide their names and how they are connected to the case and a brief
summary of what they will say.  This matter was confirmed for a trial beginning
November 25, 2024.

[
10
]

It
is quite clear from this summary that this case was intensively case managed
and that every effort was made to have the mother participate in the trial. The
mother did not serve or file an Answer to any of the three Applications. (The
father did not file an Answer to the last two wherein he agreed with the
society’s request that the child be placed with him firstly under supervision
and then by way of a s. 102 order). It was always understood that the mother’s
position was that she wanted the child returned to her immediately.

[
11
]

The
initial Application was issued on December 1, 2023. No child protection finding
has been made. The child was six when the Application was issued. The
CYFSA

requires that this matter be scheduled for trial as soon as possible. It is
noted that the child was never in care but by the terms of the February 20,
2024 order he was removed from the primary care of his mother to be placed in
the primary care of his father. There was a lot of third-party information that
had accumulated in the months prior to the issuance of the Application and the
months leading up to trial.

[
12
]

There
was a plan for this matter to be heard on the September sittings of this court.
That trial date had to be abandoned when the mother was not prepared for any of
the conferences leading up to it. A new trial date was set on August 20, 2024.
Ms. Stewart was appointed as
amicus curiae
on September 18. The mother
had counsel available to her to assist her for 3 months leading up to this
trial.

[
13
]

The
mother said she tried to file her “evidence” but the court kept rejecting it.
It is apparent that the documents that the mother tried to file were not
documents that could be filed under the
Family Law Rules
or documents
that had been authorized for filing by the case management justice. The mother
did not serve any documents that were capable of being filed prior to the
trial.

[
14
]

Time
is of the essence in child protection proceedings. A court must hold a trial on
a contested child protection finding issue as soon as possible. The mother did
not cooperate with the court in August but just insisted that she wanted her
trial in September. Now that she has had three more months to prepare she wants
an adjournment.

[
15
]

This
matter will not be adjourned.

Accommodations for the self-represented mother

[
16
]

All
counsel made it clear from the outset of trial that they wanted the mother to
be able to participate in the trial. To that end they said they were prepared
to extend deadlines for her filings. The only consideration was that each party
have a reasonable opportunity to prepare for the mother’s evidence and that the
amount of witnesses permitted to be called by the mother not exceed the five
witnesses set by Justice Cheung at the October 16 TMC.

[
17
]

The
TMC timelines were first set out in the September 18 order. The mother and

amicus
were given until November 12 to serve their trial documents. TMC
briefs, if not already filed, had to be filed by the October 16 final TMC.

[
18
]

On
October 16 the deadline remained unchanged for the mother. All other parties
identified their witnesses and time estimates were set out. As noted the mother
was present but did not participate.

[
19
]

The
matter proceeded to the trial audit of November 6. At that time the mother said
she would have 15 witnesses. The issue was briefly discussed and Justice Cheung
held that the mother could have up to 5 witnesses (subject to the discretion of
the trial judge) provided that she provided their names and a will say
statement by November 20.

[
20
]

The
mother did not meet the deadline and no witnesses were identified prior to the
opening of the trial on November 25. At that time the mother said she still intended
upon calling 15 witnesses. On consent the deadline for providing names of
potential witnesses was extended to the next morning. On November 26 the mother
still had not provided a list and she was granted a further extension to
November 27.

[
21
]

On
the morning of November 27 the mother provided a handwritten list of 15
witnesses that she insisted upon calling. There were no will say statements but
the role of each witness, i.e. professional or personal friend, was identified.

[
22
]

The
undersigned reviewed the list with the mother to see if it could be narrowed
down with her consent. She insisted that all of her witnesses were necessary.
Ultimately the undersigned held that to be consistent with the TMC direction
she could call two professional witnesses who had relevant evidence on issues
before the court and up to three friends. The mother did not agree but it was
arranged that Dr. Handley-Derry a developmental pediatrician could be called by
Zoom on November 29 as his report, released on November 22, 2023, was in the
documents brief. The mother could also call a supervisor from Brayden
Supervision Services if she could provide that supervisor with the dates of the
relevant supervised exchanges (the notes of over two years of supervised
exchanges were never ordered but the OCL clinician in the domestic matter had
recently released some). The mother then had six personal witnesses. She was
told to contact all six and if they could be available on the afternoon of
November 28 after 11 a.m. or on November 29 at least three of them could be
called.

[
23
]

As
it happened the mother had no record of the specific days she wanted to
cross-examine the Brayden supervisor about so she was not called. The mother
was able to get three of her personal witnesses who were available by November
29 and they were called.

[
24
]

In
the course of their evidence two of the personal witnesses were permitted to
read from notes that they had prepared in advance. It appeared that those notes
may have been some of the “evidence” that the mother had said she had been
prevented from filing.

[
25
]

The
mother gave her own evidence in this matter. There was a short afternoon break
and on the return the mother refused to be cross-examined. She reiterated that
the denial of her adjournment motion was unjust and that she had not had time
to prepare. She said she had no obligation to prove the case.

[
26
]

The
undersigned once again confirmed that the burden of proof was upon the society
in this trial. However. if a party chooses to give evidence then they must be
available for cross-examination. The mother refused so the issues was deferred
to the next day.

Second trial motion

[
27
]

The
trial resumed the next day November 28 and the mother filed a Motion Form. In
the motion form she stated:

I was compelled to testify on November 27, 2024 during which
I objected to providing evidence due to procedural denials of my right to file
affidavits or motions.

My testimony, as presented, substitutes for the inability to
file written evidence and should remain in record as my position in this
matter.

I assert my right to silence and refuse to answer questions
from the Applicant or any other parties, as I am not obligated to assist them
in proving their case.

My objection is grounded in the
Charter
,
the
Child
Youth and Family Services Act
and procedural fairness principles.

[
28
]

The
mother then refused to be cross-examined the next day. The undersigned noted
that given the mother’s presentation, and her insistence upon her right to be
heard without her evidence being tested, that counsel should consider how an
inability to cross-examine might prejudice their case.

[
29
]

Ms.
O’Connor said that if the mother did not give evidence she could not ask her to
identify the police and medical records that she wanted to have made exhibits
in this matter. The other counsel said that if those documents, which were in
the production briefs, could be introduced then they would also waive the right
to cross-examine.

[
30
]

The
undersigned noted that a police report often contains hearsay and cannot be
presumptively admitted for the truth of its contents. However, in all of the
circumstances of this matter the undersigned accepted the police reports and
the medical reports (mostly E.R. attendances in February 2024) as exhibits. The
mother was then not required to take the stand for cross-examination and her
direct evidence was admitted.

POSITIONS OF THE PARTIES

Children’s Aid Society of Peel  (“PCAS”) position

[
31
]

Mr.
Williams said that statutory and protection finding need to be made. The child
has lived with the father since February 2024. The child has thrived under the
care of his father. If a finding is made the disposition sought is a s.102
custody order which will affirm the current arrangement.

Father’s position

[
32
]

Ms.
O’Connor stated that the father supports a finding and the society position.
She noted that all disposition issues are in dispute. She prepared a draft
order with the specific relief the father is seeking.  Ms. O’Connor said that
there were four distinct periods of time that will be covered in the evidence.

1)

The parties
parenting roles from the birth of the child in […] 2017 through the separation
in June 6, 2020.

2)  June 2,
2022 when the first parenting order was made in the SCJ to March 28/23 when the
child was removed by the mother from his public school in Mississauga.

3)  March
28, 2023 to February 20, 2024 when the PCAS was involved over parenting issues
through the issuance of an Application and a supervision order with the mother
on December 13, 2023.

4)

February 20,
2024 when an order placed the child with the father to the opening of this
trial.

OCL

[
33
]

Ms.
Leonard as counsel for  S.W.W. supported the society position. She said that
the evidence will show that S.W.W. has been subjected to far too many
investigations and examinations. S.W.W. had been placed under a lot of stress.
He has been caught in the middle between his parents. He had taken to repeating
his mother’s statements but his demeanour and context of his statements about
his mother and his father are important.

Ms. Stewart

[
34
]

Amicus

counsel Ms. Stewart noted that the parties have been engaged in litigation in
the Superior Court of Justice (“SCJ”) since shortly after the June 2020
separation. After two OCL reports and the intervening child protection
proceedings a trial had now been scheduled in the SCJ for January 2026.

[
35
]

The
parties had a parenting schedule by September 2021 by which S.W.W. was with his
father from Friday after school until Sunday early afternoons. There were
changes made over time. Brayden Supervision services became involved and the
child left daycare or school to be exchanged with the father at 11:45 a.m. on
Fridays. Sometimes the father returned him to school and sometimes he did not.

[
36
]

The
society brought a protection application returnable December 13, 2023. A
without prejudice order was made that day by Justice M. Cheung placing S.W.W.
in the care of his mother subject to supervision with a continuation of weekend
parenting time with his father. A Temporary Care and Custody Hearing was held
on February 20, 2024.

[
37
]

The
society’s original Protection Application had sought placement with the mother
with a 6-month supervision order with the society. The father had sought
placement of the child with him. Justice L. Rogers ordered that the child
should be placed with the father with the mother to have supervised access.

[
38
]

Ms.
Stewart said that as the child had either exclusively or primarily resided with
the mother since birth the mother went into the Temporary Care hearing without
contemplating that her care of the child could change especially since the
society supported placement with her.

[
39
]

Counsel
then said that the evidence will show that the mother had been unable to get
documents before the court that she said were her “evidence’ in this matter.
Part of counsel’s role was to assist the mother to get evidence before the
court. Counsel conceded that the mother had not complied with the orders made
by Justice Cheung at the Trial Management Conference and the Trial Audit.

[
40
]

Ms.
Stewart said that the society and father’s position that parenting time with
the mother should be left in his discretion was not in the best interests of
the child. There was serious conflict between the parents. The evidence will
show that if parenting time is left to the father it will not happen. This
could destroy any relationship between the child and his mother. The mother had
been the child’s primary caregiver for most of his life. There was a close bond
between them at that time. The last few months have been very difficult for the
mother and no doubt for the child as well. The mother believes that the society
and father planned to take her child away and she is focused on that loss.

[
41
]

Ms.
Stewart told the court that the evidence will show that the mother has done
well with supervised access at the society in that she was always ready for her
visits, brings food and activities and her love and affection for the child
cannot be questioned. Ms. Stewart said that if ultimate decision is to leave
the child with the father any parenting time order should be for scheduled
supervised visits. Ms. Leonard for the OCL agreed with this point.

PROCEDURAL RULINGS

Child’s statements

[
42
]

Prior
to evidence being received counsel identified that they would be looking to
tender out of court statements made by the child for their truth of their contents.
Such statements are presumptively hearsay and not admissible.

[
43
]

To
address the issue of child’s statements the Supreme Court of Canada articulated
what is known as the principled exception to the rule against hearsay in the
well-known case of
Khan v. R.,

1990 CanLII 77 (SCC)
, 1990 CarswellOnt 108. The first question
to be determined is whether the reception of the hearsay statement is
reasonably necessary. At paragraph [31] in
Khan
,
the Supreme Court said
that:

The inadmissibility of the child's evidence might be one
basis for a finding of necessity. But sound evidence based on psychological
assessments that testimony in court might be traumatic for the child or harm
the child might also serve. There may be other examples of circumstances which
would establish requirement of necessity.

[
44
]

The
next part of the test is whether the proposed evidence meets the test of
threshold reliability. Threshold reliability is established when the hearsay is
sufficiently reliable to overcome the dangers arising from the difficulty of
testing it. The hearsay dangers relate to the difficulties of assessing the
child’s perception, memory, narration or sincerity. These dangers can be
overcome by showing that (1) there are adequate substitutes for testing truth
and accuracy (procedural reliability) or (2) that there are sufficient
circumstantial or evidentiary guarantees that the statement is inherently
trustworthy (substantive reliability).

[
45
]

The
trial judge acts as a gatekeeper for determining threshold reliability and
leaves the ultimate determination of whether a statement is reliable for the
finding of facts. See:
R. v. Khelawon
,
2006 SCC 57
.

[
46
]

In
this case Ms. Leonard for the OCL prepared a chart of the child’s statements
that counsel sought to have admitted, some for the truth of their contents, and
some for the fact that they were said. The chart set out the date of the
statement, the recipient of the statement and the purpose for which it was
sought to be introduced.

[
47
]

The
proper approach to determine necessity and threshold reliability is to hold a
voir
dire
, a trial within a trial, to determine if the proposed evidence is
admissible. As there were many statements made to different witnesses the approach
adopted was to test the admissibility of the statements made to each witness
but not to make a ruling on admissibility until all of the trial evidence was
received.

[
48
]

I
find that all of the statements made to a child protection worker or other
professional required to gather and record information were admissible for the
fact that they were said by the child. The child made many inconsistent
statements and frequently retracted statements made earlier. The reason that
this happened is explored below. Ultimately there had to be a determination of
whether the statements were likely true of false. The child’s statements were
just part of the evidence that had to be considered. The statements must be
looked at the context of the other evidence that was available around the time
each statement was made.

Trial worthy affidavits

[
49
]

The
society witnesses were required to provide their direct evidence by way of
affidavit. All four counsel reviewed every affidavit in advance and they agreed
upon any redactions that should be made to make the evidence trial worthy. The
court thanks counsel for their cooperation which saved valuable trial time.

EVIDENCE

Terri-Lynn
Noble

[
50
]

Ms.
Noble had been the principal at C.H.P.S. since March 2020. She had been a
teacher for 25 years and had taken a number of additional qualification courses
over the years.

[
51
]

Ms.
Noble first met the child with his mother when he started junior kindergarten
(“J.K.”). She had observed S.W.W. in the classroom over all three years that he
had attended her school. He attended C.H.P.S. for his J.K. and Grade 1 and 2
years. He attended F.A.P.S. for his senior kindergarten (“S.K.”) year.

[
52
]

Ms.
Noble took a very active role supporting the classroom teachers such that she
is informed about children with behavioural issues. In fact she set up a desk
just outside S.W.W.’s classroom so she could personally observe what was going
on.

[
53
]

In
J.K., S.W.W. only attended for half days at his mother’s insistence. The child
went to a different school for S.K. but returned to her school for Grade 1. The
mother insisted on being with him at the school for the start of the year. Ms.
Noble noted that the child was frequently disruptive in class and often did not
listen to the teacher.  He tried unsuccessfully to make friends. He was pulled
out of school by his mother from time to time.

[
54
]

Ms.
Noble said that S.W.W’s Grade 2 year that began in September 2024 has been much
better. He has attended regularly and he was able to interact with friends. He
is now becoming a leader amongst his peers and he is much more settled.

[
55
]

The
principal was referred to the child’s report cards. They showed:

June 28/22 – C.H.P.S. – 53.5
days absent and 24 days late – the child lived with the mother

June 27/23 – F.A.P.S. – 68.5
days absent and 44 days late – child lived with the mother

[
56
]

Ms.
Noble stated that that in the period September 2023 to February 20, 2024 when
the child lived with the mother he was only present in school for 49 out of 104
days. The principal said that there were different doctor’s notes for many of
the absences.

[
57
]

Ms.
Noble admitted that while in the father’s care after February 20/24 the child
was only absent for two full days and two half days as a result of illness.

[
58
]

The
principal said that while S.W.W. was in his mother’s care it was difficult to
deal with the child. She said that he would not listen. He was very combative.
He wanted to please his mother so he told her things that did not happen at
school. This caused the mother to come to the school. Often with the child
beside her she confronted Ms Noble. The mother would always bring the child
into the argument and she encouraged him to tell the principal negative things
about the school such as the teacher is picking on him and always yelling at
him. If the child said he was doing well the mother told him he was not and
blamed the school for that.

[
59
]

In
his J.K. year his mother decided that he should attend for half days as she
wanted him to go home for a nap. The principal could not prevent that but said that
it was clear that the child wanted to be in school.

[
60
]

Ms.
Noble said the entire experience was hard for the child and hard for the school
staff. Ms. Noble said that S.W.W. is now a confident child and happy to be at
school. Since he has been under his father’s care he is excited to be with his
friends and he is enjoying school as he should. In his Grade 1 year the child
was registered as having Autism Spectrum Disorder (“A.S.D.”) and as such he had
access to more resources though he did not use them.

[
61
]

The
mother was very focused on the supports, or lack of same, provided to her son.
In 2023 Ms. Nobel was made aware by the father that a private
psycho-educational report had been completed. Dr. Ewa Antczak prepared the

provided by Ms. Friesen or other advocates with their own agendas.

[
309
]

The mother then
returned to her point that the child had always lived with her, she had
lovingly cared for him and it would cause her son emotional harm to continue to
kept from her primary care. She said she had met all of the child’s needs.

[
310
]

Ms. Leonard and
Ms. Stewart made submissions on both the child protection and the disposition
issues.

[
311
]

The parties made
submissions on all issues. In following the statutory pathway I will consider
the evidence concerning the risk of emotional harm before considering any
evidence that relates to disposition.

ANALYSIS OF EMOTIONAL HARM ISSUE

Pre-separation
evidence.

[
312
]

The society was
not involved with the family prior to the separation. The mother’s evidence was
that she was the child’s primary parent. The father worked long hours. She gave
evidence that the father was abusive to her. The father denied this. The father
was acquitted after the Crown recommended to the court a not guilty verdict. An
acquittal in a criminal court on specific charges does not mean that there was
not coercive control or abuse in the relationship.

[
313
]

This case was
not about what happened in the party’s marriage prior to separation. There are
two completely different narratives. The father was not asked to comment upon
the mother’s evidence. He did say that when he worked he was at home a lot as
he only worked four days a week. He noted that he was also laid off for
extensive periods. He said that on his days off and in the long periods of
lay-off despite he was an active and involved father.

[
314
]

The only part of
the pre-separation evidence that is relevant to the issue of a finding is that
the child was always in the primary care of the mother. The child was healthy
when born but as he grew older there was a concern that his speech and language
were delayed. The mother was very protective of her son and a very strong
advocate for him.

Projection of anxiety

[
315
]

Throughout the
period from the first society involvement to the trial the mother seemed
determined to prove that she had not physically abused her son. There was never
an allegation that she did. The mother seemed not to be able to understand that
the concern was not that she did not care about her son but that she was
hyper-focused on seeking solutions to problems that may not exist.

[
316
]

The
pre-separation phase showed that both parents might have some mental health
challenges. The mother said that the father was depressed and took pills. The
father did speak of the challenges in his marriage and his difficulty in
coping. He said he sought help and had been taking medication that was very
beneficial and allowed him to work full time and be a good caregiver to his
son.

[
317
]

The mother did
not concede that she had any emotional or mental health challenges. She said
she was the victim of an abusive marriage and was solely focused on her son’s
many needs. She had no insight into the fact that she was the common denominator
in the many conflicts that she had with medical and educational professionals.

[
318
]

The mother
always presented as extremely anxious. When the child began J.K. she wanted to
attend school every day with the child. When that was not permitted she insisted
that he had to come home at lunch time for a nap when all of the other children
stayed at school. She had no insight into the fact that she was making it more
difficult for her son at school because of all of the attention she was drawing
towards him. There was no recommendation by medical or educational
professionals for the child to only attend for half days. On the contrary, the
fact that his speech and language was behind meant that he needed to be in
school getting help and interacting with other children.

[
319
]

The evidence is
clear that the mother projected her own needs and anxieties onto the child.
Even the mother’s best friend G.R. described her as “overly protective” of the
child.

[
320
]

The mother
became convinced that the child must have autism. She actively sought out a
diagnosis. The family doctor eventually referred to her to a pediatrician Dr.
Kao who had a 45 minute video interview with the three to four year old child
in 2021. He diagnosed S.W.W. with A.S.D. level two or three. He also diagnosed him
with A.D.H.D.

[
321
]

After the child
was registered in J.K. the mother was adamant that her son was not receiving
the educational assistance he needed. The mother went to the family doctor’s
office numerous times to obtain letters for the school to request further
assistance. The nurse practitioner became concerned that the letters were
really just the mother’s words on the doctor’s letterhead and thought that
their office was being used to fuel the mother’s agenda.

[
322
]

The child went
to J.K. at C.H.P.S. because the mother was then living in the condominium owned
by the father that became the matrimonial home. By September 2022 the father
was back in that condo and the mother was living in a different apartment. The
child was then registered at F.A.P.S. for his S.K. year. There was no evidence
directly from the principal at that school but the report cards were filed. The
mother kept the child out of school repeatedly during that year. Eventually in
March 2023 she chose to withdraw him from public school.

[
323
]

The mother
failed to advise the father of where his son was going to school or if he was
going to school. It was disclosed at trial that the mother had taken him to a
private religious school in Markham. She was convinced that the public schools
were never going to give her son what he needed. She sought out advice from a
priest who recommended that she move to New Hamburg to attend a small religious
school where S.W.W. could get more individual attention.

Conflict over education and supports for child

[
324
]

During this time
the litigation in the SCJ. was continuing and the father sought a
psycho-educational assessment as he did not believe that his son had A.S.D or
that he could not obtain the resources he needed in the public system. The
mother opposed a psycho-educational assessment. She also opposed the child
returning to public school.

[
325
]

A court order
was made in September 2023 that S.W.W. return to C.H.P.S. The
psycho-educational report of Dr. E. Antczak was concluded and the psychologist
did not think that the child had A.S.D .but she did think he had A.D.H.D and
learning difficulties.

[
326
]

The mother
remained convinced that her son had A.S.D. I find that she refused to send him
to school in the fall of 2023. He had 41 absences from school between September
and December 2023. This continued a pattern of not sending the child to school.
He missed 53.5 days and was late 24 days in his J.K. year at C.H.P.S. In his
S.K. year at F.A.P.S the child was absent 68.5 days and late 44 days and that
was only until March 2023 when the mother pulled him out of school.

[
327
]

Throughout all
of this time the mother took the position that the child was very anxious and
was afraid of going to school. She said that the child was being bullied at
school by other children and assaulted by his teachers. The mother points to
the child confirming this in interviews with the workers and others. I find as
a fact that the child was not being abused by the teachers and there is no
credible evidence that he was particularly picked on by other students.

[
328
]

The evidence was
that the mother went to the school on thirty occasions between September 7,
2023 and February 9, 2024. She also went there on January 9, 16, 29 and 24.
These were contentious meetings between the mother and the principal or
teachers that took place in front of the child.

[
329
]

In that same
period the mother began taking the child to the E.R. Her family doctor would
not allow her to make further appointments for non-physical matters so she took
the child to the hospital instead. In S.W.W.’s presence she tried to get
doctors to support her contention that the child was too anxious or frightened
to attend school. The visits became more frequent as the temporary care hearing
approached. There were five separate visits to the E.R. between February 1 and
19, 2024.

Consequences
of conflict in front of child

[
330
]

It may be that
the mother could not help herself from seeking ways to justify keeping S.W.W.
out of school because of her fixed delusions about what was happening to her
son there. It may also be that she was attempting to record evidence on her
phone for use in the court battle. Either way the child was exposed to this
conflict and it caused him emotional harm as he refused to make eye contact and
was stuttering when called upon by the mother to support her. I find that had
the child continued to reside with the mother further emotional harm would no
doubt have resulted.

[
331
]

I find that the
mother was so focused on protecting her son she actually made his life much
more difficult. The mother became convinced that she was the only one who
really saw what was happening to her son. She refused to believe any evidence
that did not fit into her narrative. She constantly sought out opinions that
would support her beliefs. She felt that only she knew what was best for S.W.W.

[
332
]

The mother was
pleased to get a diagnosis of A.S.D. from Dr. Kao and angry and frustrated when
that diagnosis did not lead to the special treatment for her son that she was
convinced he required. The mother wanted to be at the school with her son
because she saw herself as his protector. She had no insight into how her
hyper-vigilance would impact upon her son’s emotional health.

[
333
]

In fact, because
of the mother’s hyper vigilance the school principal saw the child every day.
She even set up her desk outside of his classroom. She knew the mother would
continue to make allegations and she wanted to know exactly what was, and what
was not, happening. She also wanted to support her teachers whom she knew would
be accused of wrongdoing.

[
334
]

I found the
evidence of Ms. Noble the principal of C.H.P.S. to have been very helpful. She
is a very experienced educator and she understood immediately the issues that
her school was facing. She made a point of getting to know S.W.W. She observed
him daily. She is not a medical professional so she was unable to provide an opinion
on what, if any, disorders the child might have. However, I am convinced that
she and the teachers at her school considered S.W.W’s needs at every step. The
fact that the child fell behind academically was no fault of the school. I
accept the preponderance of expert evidence that S.W.W. had learning challenges
but those challenges had a profound negative impact upon his academic
achievement not because of a lack of resources but because of the mother’s
failure to send him to school.

[
335
]

I find that S.W.W.
did not have any significant anxieties about attending school. Once he was
living with his father he attended school every day. The result was that his
marks improved dramatically. The mother said that her son was bullied at school
but when he was with his father he easily made friends and even became a mentor
to another student who was anxious.

[
336
]

The mother’s
complete failure to meet her son’s educational needs by keeping him from school
had already caused the child emotional harm in the form of delayed development.

[
337
]

Once the child
was with his father, and in school, a real effort was made by the father and
the society to get him help. Mr. Kennedy is not an expert in child development
but he is an experienced counsellor. His observation was that when he first saw
the child he was withdrawn and defiant but over time he calmed down and they
formed a good therapeutic relationship. I find that if the child had remained
in his mother’s care he would have been at risk of further withdrawal and even
self-destructive behaviour.

[
338
]

While the mother
was frequently observed to be aggressive and confrontational with the society
workers and at the school she had another side that was apparent even in court.
The mother could be quiet and polite and despite her very obsessive nature she
appeared genuinely interested in obtaining help for her son. Her entire life
was invested in her son’s well-being and her devotion to him, and her
willingness to advocate for him, despite obstacles could have made her seem not
only passionate but credible in providing S.W.W.’s story.

[
339
]

The undersigned
is not able to say that the child does not have A.S.D. It can only be concluded
that whatever specific diagnosis he might have the child failed academically
when living with his mother and made great gains in the year when he was living
with his father. The one clear difference was that the child missed an
inordinate amount of school when with his mother and did not miss school when
with his father. The mother’s action in not sending her son to school and
pulling him out of school would likely have caused the emotional harm of
delayed development had it continued.

Frequent reports and investigations

[
340
]

Prior to the
society becoming re-involved in March 2023 there had been bitter litigation
ongoing in the SCJ since shortly after the separation. There were countless
allegations made. The mother did not agree to even supervised visits with the
father for the first 7 months after the separation.

[
341
]

The OCL were
asked to become involved on three separate occasions.  Ms. Majewski did an
interim report on July 27, 2022 and a discontinued report on March 17, 2023
before the society was even re-involved. This required interviewing the child
on a number of occasions and seeing him with each parent.

[
342
]

The society
became involved with this family again once the mother stopped co-operating
with the OCL and pulled the child out of school. Ms. O’Connor the father’s
counsel said that since March 2023 a worker from the PCAS interviewed the child
on 42 separate occasions.

[
343
]

In each case the
mother made an allegation based upon something she said that the child told
her. They included the teacher’s grabbing his arm, the PGM and then the
paternal uncle denying the child food and water and locking him in a closet.
The child was then interviewed. When the mother demanded he make statements
when she was present he looked to her and after she nodded he made a statement
consistent with what she had reported. He was observed to be reluctant to talk
and even stuttering on some occasions.

[
344
]

There was
evidence that the child made negative statements about his father almost by
rote without emotion but then after seeing his father S.W.W. retracted any
negative statements about him. I find that these statements made in the
presence of the mother, or reported to have been made to the mother with no one
else present, are not admissible for their truth of their contents. However,
the statements made in front of PCAS workers are admissible for the fact that
they were made.

[
345
]

Ms. O’Connor
noted that the mother made eight E.R. visits seeking psychiatric referrals for
her son. There were nine reports to the Peel police that the child was being
abused. The child was interviewed for eight of them. There were two calls to
EveryMind crisis counselling. The mother engaged Dr. Handley-Derry to do an
A.S.D assessment even though there was an SCJ order for no further assessments.
The child had seven video appointments with the pediatrician. This constant
questioning of the child, if it were to continue, would lead to anxiety,
withdrawal and possible even aggressive behaviour.

[
346
]

I find that the
mother was very receptive to hearing negative statements made by the child
particularly ones about his father and his treatment at school. I also find
that it is likely that the mother coached the child in that the statements that
he made fit her narrative. She had felt since prior to the 2020 separation that
the father and his family disliked her and were determined to take her child
away from her. She felt that her son had special needs and that only Dr. Kao,
and much later Dr. Handley-Derry, really understood that he had A.S.D and that
the school system had failed him.

[
347
]

The mother went
to Dr. Ostro’s office on 16 separate occasions often with the child with her.
Once she was told by Ms. Shinjar that she could not come anymore she began
taking S.W.W. to the Emergency Room to get support for her position. The mother
sought out a diagnosis for the child without informing the father of what she
was doing. The father never spoke to Dr. Kao or Dr. Handley-Derry. He only
became aware of the latter’s extensive testing and interviewing of his son once
her received a copy of the report from his lawyer.

[
348
]

Dr.
Handley-Derry is clearly an expert in diagnosing ASD. However, Ms. Leonard from
the OCL completed a nuanced and effective cross-examination of him. She did not
directly allege that he was biased but she was able to have him concede that
having only listened to the mother’s concerns he did not see the other side of
child. He was not aware of the bitter family law litigation or that the mother
had refused to send the child to school. He did not know of the
psycho-educational assessment.

[
349
]

The only
background the pediatrician had was from the mother and it included that
another pediatrician Dr. Kao had diagnosed her son to have A.S.D. yet the
educational system had not provided resources for him and consequently he was
falling behind. I did not find Dr. Handley-Derry’s evidence to be helpful.

Negative statements and conflict

[
350
]

Once the society
became involved it soon became apparent that the mother had no inhibitions
about making negative statements about the father in front of the child. The
child was observed to be very uncomfortable when she made these statements.

[
351
]

The mother was
very prepared for her access visits at the society’s offices and she was
affectionate with the child. Some visits were almost entirely positive and the
child enjoyed him. At other times though the mother came into conflict with the
society workers and raised her voice with them in front of the child. The
workers could see how anxious the child became when this happened and they
tried to re-direct her but once she became worked up she could not be
re-directed. The child would then be observed to be pleading with his mother to
stop what she was doing and instead play with him. The society workers would
observe the child to become sad after visits. The child has even apologized for
the mother’s behaviour on a few occasions after visits. The father said that
the child was quite happy after some visits and sad and withdrawn after others.

[
352
]

It became
apparent that the mother’s desperate need to have others support her in her
battle with the father and the society led her to rely upon some people who had
their own agendas to pursue. The mother was accompanied to visits by others and
while at visits she made phone calls to others. G.R. appeared to try to
re-direct the mother when he went but when the mother was not accompanied by
him she became very upset and she would call “Ramona” for advice. Ramona
Friesen’s evidence showed that she saw the mother as someone who is being
abused by an unjust system.

[
353
]

The mother’s
frustrations with the school system led her to seek out like-minded people even
before the society became involved. There is no evidence before me that the
mother has a mental health diagnosis and no evidence that she has ever sought
out personal therapy or treatment. However, her actions were often bizarre and
irrational and they demonstrated some paranoid thinking. As noted above there
were periods when the mother was able to remain calm and when she was pleasant
and polite just as there were access visits that went very positively. On the
other hand, the mother was completely unable or unwilling to follow any court
orders concerning this trial and she was unable to stop herself from making
non-sensical objections that appeared to be founded in the kind of thinking set
out in Ms. Friesen’s statement.

[
354
]

The mother’s
apparent untreated mental health issues have caused the child to suffer a
significant amount of stress. He did make statements that his mother is acting
“crazy” and he was frustrated and sad that he could not do anything about it.
If the child lived with the mother and she did not seek treatment for her
obvious mental disorder this would risk emotional harm to the child in the form
of anxiety, depression and withdrawal.

Decision

[
355
]

I find that the
society has satisfied the burden upon them to prove that if the child had not
been removed from the mother’s care that he would have been at risk of
emotional harm. I find that there was evidence that some emotional harm had
already been caused. Fortunately, as will be noted in the disposition section
of these reasons there has been a mitigation of that harm since the child has
been in his father’s care.

[
356
]

I find that the
child cannot be returned to the mother who had charge of him prior to society
intervention. I find that the society has provided assistance to the mother by
way of consistent supervised visits initially twice per week for four hours.
Due to her fixed belief that there was never any need for society involvement
she has not only been unreceptive to society assistance but she had often been
argumentative and confrontational with society staff.

[
357
]

Ms. Stewart
noted in her submission that it appeared that the mother’s lack of insight was
not “voluntary”. The mother had objected to any statement that she had any
mental health issues. Nevertheless, it may be that if the mother had sought
professional help for what certainly presents as a mental health disorder this
matter might have had a different trajectory.

ANALYSIS OF DISPOSITION ISSUE

The father’s care of the child

[
358
]

The child was
placed in the care of the father on February 20, 2024 after a temporary care
and custody hearing before Justice L. Rogers and he has remained in his care
since. The father has ensured that the child has attended school daily. The
father and the child have had the benefit of a counsellor Mr. Kennedy who comes
to their home every week. His evidence was that the child was initially
withdrawn and reluctant to talk but over time they developed a good relationship.
He still meets with the child. Mr. Kennedy has also provided parenting tips to
the father which the father has implemented with some success.

[
359
]

The father has
been laid off from work for some time so he has a lot of time to spend with his
son. He has worked with S.W.W. on his literacy and the principal stated that
the child had improved dramatically. In fact, the school no longer needs to
provide any additional support for S.W.W. now that he is thriving in a regular
classroom. Far from being anxious about school the child looks forward to
attending even packing his things for Monday morning when he gets home from
school on Friday.

[
360
]

The father has
involved his son in extra-curricular activities and they are well connected to
their community. In fact the father had planned to move to Durham region (where
the parties had lived when the child was young) to be closer tohis anticipated
work but he has chosen not to relocate at this time so that he can keep
continuity and stability for the child.

The mother’s plan

[
361
]

The mother said
that she wanted her son returned to her immediately. The court must order a
return to the parent who had charge of the child prior to its intervention
unless it is not in the child’s best interests to do so.

[
362
]

For reasons
stated, I find that it is not in the child’s best interests to live with his
mother. The reasons for society’s involvement have not been addressed. The
mother continues to have fixed delusions that her child is being harmed at
school and that his needs are not being met. She was unable to prepare the
necessary documents for this trial and she was unable to control her behaviour
to the point where she had to be asked to leave the courtroom. She refused to
be subjected to cross-examination and she parroted legal documents that appear
to have been provided to her by persons who have taken advantage of her
legitimate distress and fears to advance their own agenda (which agenda may in
itself have taken root as a result of their own personal traumas).

[
363
]

The mother has
demonstrated that she loves her child and that she is affectionate with him.
She knows how to engage him in play and she clearly wants what is best for him.
The mother has shown herself to be intelligent and well organized. She never
missed an access visit and she always arrived with appropriate food and
activities.

[
364
]

The mother has
not had an easy life. She arrived in Canada with her former husband whom she
met in Russia. Her parents died before she left home and she has no family in
Canada and it appears few friends until after the separation. She has shown the
ability to be a good friend to O.M. and G.R. Sadly, the mother has a fixed
belief that when her son is not in her direct care he is being abused, bullied,
mistreated or abandoned.

[
365
]

This trial has
shown that the “facts” upon which the mother relies for her beliefs do not
exist or have been manipulated to suite her narrative. It is to be hoped that
the mother will eventually develop some insight and seek help. In the interim
it is important that all steps possible are taken for S.W.W. to have a positive
relationship with his mother. The mother needs that and her son deserves it.

Parenting time with the mother

[
366
]

The society’s
initial position was that after a s.102 custody order is made the mother’s
parenting time should be at the discretion of the father. The father, the OCL
and the
amicus
counsel thought that the parents would need assistance in
organizing parenting time. The society then changed its position so that all
parties except the mother supported an order for the mother to have supervised
parenting time with the child at a supervised parenting time centre.

[
367
]

The preferred
position of all parties, except the mother and the society, was for the society
to continue to facilitate parenting time once per week. The society stated that
it would facilitate access pending the receipt of the final order and for up to
six weeks after that until the parties could transition to a supervised
facility. The society even stated that it would consider an extension to that
and when the OCL sought 10 weeks post-order there was no objection.

[
368
]

Notwithstanding
all of the conflict that has occurred at the society’s visit centre the fact
remains that there have been some very positive visits that are of real benefit
to the child. When the visits have descended into conflict the child at least
knows that he is physically safe as when the visit time ends his father will
pick him up. There is no doubt that continuing visits at the society visit
centre would be best for the child and for his parents. That said, the society
has limited resources and their visit centre is needed for open child
protection cases. It is not the society’s mandate to provide visits for
children who are in the custody of one of their parents.

[
369
]

The mother did
not comment upon parenting time as she did not want to contemplate a situation
in which her son is not returned to her. She did say that if S.W.W. was with
her she would be willing to share time with the father.

[
370
]

I find that the
following factors must be considered when considering what parenting time order
to make for the period beyond which the society can offer services. They are:

a)

It is in the
child’s best interests to have once a week visits with his mother.

b)

Unless the
mother’s mental health improves to the point where she can exercise  frequent
positive visits with the child the visits will remain supervised.

c)  If the
mother is able to have positive visits free of conflict the parties could move
to non-professional supervisors
.

d)

If the mother
continues to have paranoid fixations with professional supervisors she will
either not be able to qualify for the Peel Supervised Parenting Time program or
the visits will be cancelled or suspended there leaving a gap when there are no
lawyers or social workers readily available to help restore parenting time.

e)

The court should
not make final orders for supervised parenting time at a Ministry of the
Attorney General site as those sites have waiting lists and need to have
availability to serve new families. Supervised visits are a stepping-stone to
non-supervised visits.

[
371
]

Weighing the
factors set out above I find that the best path forward is to make a flexible
order that can adapt to changed circumstances without a return to court.

[
372
]

The order will
be for the parties to immediately register for supervised parenting time with
the P.S.P.T program. They shall accept the first available time slot in the
Mississauga location. The mother shall pay for the cost of supervision. The
parties shall use fully supervised visits for a maximum period of one year
unless P.S.P.T can offer further service. If at any time the parties can agree
upon another supervisor then they may move from P.S.P.T fully supervised
services. They will then have the option to engage the P.S.P.T supervised
exchange service for as long as it is needed.

[
373
]

If the parties
are not accepted by the P.S.P.T. program or want to avoid a wait list and get
longer visits the mother can opt to pay for a private supervision service such
as Brayden Supervision Services. The parties are familiar with Brayden as it
was used for the father to have visits before they became unsupervised.

[
374
]

If the mother
obtains a mental health assessment and complies with a treatment plan she may propose
that a non-professional third party supervise or facilitate the visits. In that
event, she shall provide the background and parenting experience of the
proposed supervisor and offer the father an opportunity to meet with her at a
public location. If the father does not agree to use the private supervisor he
shall provide reasons in writing through a parenting application. If he does
agree to use the private supervisor then the child shall be exchanged between
the supervisor and the father without the mother present.

[
375
]

If at any time
the father is prepared to agree to the mother having unsupervised parenting
time it can be arranged though it would be best if a transition to that
occurred by using the supervised exchange program at P.S.P.T or by an exchange
with a third party. It may be that parenting time can gradually transition if
there are continued positive visits.

[
376
]

The parties
cannot use a MAG site for supervised parenting time if there is any other
parenting time occurring and that includes video parenting time. If there have
been a serios of positive parenting time visits, and the parties are not using
a MAG site, then video parenting time should be introduced.

[
377
]

With respect to
communication between the parties the father’s evidence was that he thought
that the parties should communicate about S.W.W. on a frequent basis. When he
was asked by Ms. Stewart if he was prepared to provide a monthly update the
father said that that seemed too long and the communication should be at least
weekly. The father appeared to struggle in his evidence to differentiate what
he wished would happen and what he realistically could expect would happen. He
wished that the mother would address her mental health disorder so that she
could have unsupervised parenting time.  He did not expect that would happen,
at least not in the near future, but he knew that his son needed to see his
mother and he hoped that this would happen in an emotionally safe way through
continued supervised time.

COSTS

[
378
]

The father’s
counsel sought costs against the mother on a full recovery basis in the amount
of $96,500. She stated that a court can order costs against one respondent
parent in a child protection proceeding where there has been highly
unreasonable behaviour by one parent and that parent has disobeyed court orders
and shown bad faith.

[
379
]

In
Children’s
Aid Society of Halton Region v. J.S.,

2014 ONCJ 38
, Justice Roselyn Zisman
wrote that while parents should be entitled to vigorously oppose and defend
themselves in a child protection proceeding without the fear of cost sanctions,
they will not be insulated from a claim of costs if they act in bad faith, are
unreasonable or act in a manner that is disproportionate to the issues
involved. The father was ordered to pay the mother costs of $18,000.

[
380
]

In
Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. S.T.,

2018 ONCJ 573
, Justice Ellen Murray wrote
that costs should only be ordered between parents in a child protection case if
a parent has exhibited extreme unreasonable conduct. She set out examples of
extreme unreasonable conduct as being: unreasonable behaviour that harms the
children, a parent who heightens and extends conflict, a parent who repeatedly
disobeys court orders, or who misleads the court and a parent found to be
acting in bad faith
. However, she observed that even highly unreasonable
behaviour by a parent may not result in an award of costs if the behaviour
originates from mental illness, not just stubborn rigidity.

(emphasis
added)

[
381
]

This was a long
and difficult proceeding that effectively began in March 2023. The parents have
been engaged in bitter litigation since 2020 in the SCJ. Both parents are no
doubt emotionally exhausted and the father is no doubt financially exhausted as
he has had counsel in both proceedings.

[
382
]

There can be
nothing more stressful in our system of justice to any person than facing the
prospect of having your child taken from your care, or not returned to your
care after having been taken previously. Just when submissions were about to be
made the father’s counsel handed the mother’s counsel a bill of costs for
$96,500. The timing of the presentation of the bill was ill advised.

[
383
]

I will adopt the
reasoning of Justice Murray in
Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. S.T
.
(
supra).
As noted throughout these reasons the mother has acted in
irrational ways for some time. She appears to have an undiagnosed and untreated
mental health disorder. Her disorder has caused some additional pre-trial time
but I cannot find that she wilfully acted in bad faith and irresponsibly ran up
costs. Her behaviour was at times very challenging for the court, and no doubt
for the litigants, but the evidence suggests that she did not act in the way
she did to advance her position and delay and frustrate the father’s case.
Quite the opposite is true. The mother wanted to adjourn this trial when the
child had been in the father’s care for nearly a year.

[
384
]

I do not think
this is an appropriate case for costs between respondents. The society
fulfilled its legal mandate to bring this matter before the court. The society
quite properly responded to court orders and changed circumstances and amended
its applications as needed. The orders sought by the society are ones that the
father supported.

[
385
]

The society had
the onus of proof. The father completed one affidavit, prepared a document
brief and was cross-examined. It is true that the mother failed to comply with
the trial management orders in this proceeding. Her actions were irrational and
appear to be the result of her apparent mental health disorder. The court made
accommodations for the mother that were paid for out of public resources- the
most significant one being the appointment of
amicus curiae.
Ms. Stewart
was of great assistance to the court in ensuring that all relevant evidence was
received and/or challenged. Her involvement and the society’s steps to advance
this matter to trial resulted in a resolution that kept the child in the
father’s care.

[
386
]

I would not have
addressed costs in these reasons except for two points. Firstly, counsel
insisted that she was entitled to make costs submissions now to avoid a
separate submission after the trial decision was released.

[
387
]

Secondly, during
the period of this reserve the father’s counsel served and filed a motion seeking
a conference call to address fresh evidence or to grant leave to re-open the
trial to hear fresh evidence. The only party to respond to the motion was the
mother. She opposed re-opening the trial. Her affidavit then went on to
describe what has been happening post-trial. I chose not to read it as it would
not be appropriate to read it and then decide the motion without asking for the
father’s update. I dismissed the motion and provided reasons for so doing.

[
388
]

As noted in the
reasons above all counsel co-operated in reducing the length of this trial by
carefully reviewing evidence in advance and redacting that which was not trial
worthy. All counsel made significant efforts to ensure a fair trial and one
that was organized and focused. This was a case that could easily have exceeded
the six days scheduled. Counsel are to be commended for how they dealt with
this difficult matter.
